prize_parts.citation: for incorporating nominal rigidities into macroeconomics through staggered price and wage setting, policy rules and a microfounded framework for monetary policy analysis

statement.case_for: My opening view stands: B001 is the strongest candidate on common criteria of scientific originality, breadth, durability and demonstrated influence. Nominal rigidity is the central mechanism by which money and monetary policy have real effects. Calvo supplied the tractable time-dependent pricing device, Taylor the staggered-contract model and the interest-rate rule, and Woodford the integrated, welfare-based theory of policy. Together they changed both the theory and the practice of central banking. The influence is visible in the models and rules used in policy institutions, not only in citations. The work is 25 to 45 years old and has been tested through the 2008 crisis, the zero lower bound and the post-2021 inflation. The 2022 prize went to banking and financial crises, not to this core. As someone working on price-setting microfoundations, I see why the core is robust: the framework gives a disciplined account of why prices adjust slowly, which is exactly where the micro evidence on price adjustment, pass-through and menu costs connects to macro policy. The recurring Taylor, Woodford, Calvo set across the opening proposals suggests the attribution problem is less severe than the ballot's eight names imply, because a three-person core is separable by function (pricing mechanism, policy rule, normative synthesis).
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. Any three-person cut excludes contributors with substantial claims: Gali and Gertler on the canonical New Keynesian model and its empirical use, Christiano and Eichenbaum on the identified, estimated medium-scale DSGE model, and Smets on its adoption at the ECB. A second reservation comes from my own micro evidence. Price-adjustment data and surveys show a mix of time and state dependence. Calvo's device is therefore a tractable approximation rather than a literal description, and the framework's fit during the post-2021 inflation, and with heterogeneity, is genuinely debated. I regard this as a limit on the claim rather than a refutation, since the framework's value lies in organizing policy analysis and giving a benchmark that later work builds on.

responses.point: Hassler ranks Kiyotaki and Moore (B002) first for a foundational, tractable collateral-constraint mechanism. He ranks B001 third, noting that prior prizes (Phelps, Lucas, Kydland-Prescott, Sargent-Sims) narrow the unclaimed space and that the framework was challenged after 2008 and 2021.
responses.response: I agree that Kiyotaki-Moore is a clean two-author attribution and a foundational mechanism, and that is why I list B002's weaknesses as relative, not absolute. On the prior prizes, I think the unclaimed space is still real. Those awards covered expectations, time consistency and identification of policy effects. None recognised the pricing frictions, the policy-rule analysis or the microfounded normative framework that central banks use directly. B002 is also partly covered by the 2022 prize on banking and financial crises, whereas B001's core has no neighbouring recent award. I accept that the post-2008 and post-2021 criticisms are serious. But they led to extensions (heterogeneous-agent models, financial frictions) that build on this framework, which is the usual sign of a foundational contribution. I would put B002 behind B001 rather than ahead of it.

responses.point: Strömberg ranks B015 (Pakes, Berry, Levinsohn) first for the methodological reach of BLP and dynamic oligopoly estimation. He flags whether Bresnahan, or the Bresnahan-Reiss entry work, should be preferred to Levinsohn.
responses.response: I share much of this assessment, which is why B015 is my second choice and the leading alternative. As an IO economist I know how much BLP has changed merger review and welfare analysis. My ranking is not a verdict against it. The difference with B001 is breadth of conceptual influence, since B015 is predominantly a toolkit contribution and B001 changed how a whole policy domain is understood. On Bresnahan, I agree it is a close call. Pakes is clearly the strongest name, but the BLP trio is the cleanest documented attribution on this ballot and I would not add Bresnahan without a clear argument that his priority outweighs Levinsohn's co-authorship of the central paper. I also treat my own field proximity as a reason to be cautious about favouring B015, not as a reason to push it.

responses.point: Dreber Almenberg ranks B001 fifth because it is the most diffuse candidate, with eight names and overlapping contributions, and because the empirical performance of the canonical framework has been questioned.
responses.response: Diffuse attribution is the right test, and I do not dismiss it. But the opening rankings show strong convergence on the same three names: eleven of eleven proposals contain Taylor, Woodford and Calvo. In my view that reflects a functional separation (pricing mechanism, rule, normative synthesis) and not arbitrary selection. The empirical-performance concern is real. Our own work on menu costs and asymmetric adjustment shows state-dependent adjustment that the Calvo device does not capture. But the committee's task is to recognise contributions that changed the field, not to certify that a model is a literal description, and Calvo, Taylor and Woodford each supplied a component that later work, including state-dependent pricing, uses as the benchmark. If the committee concludes that attribution cannot be separated, my fallback is B021 or B015, where the credit is cleaner.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B021 (Helpman, Melitz) first because firm heterogeneity changed how trade, productivity and welfare are modelled. He notes that the empirical pioneers (Bernard, Jensen, Eaton, Kortum) are outside the entry, and that the distinctness from earlier new trade theory is a question.
responses.response: I rank B021 third and agree on its strength, including that trade has not been recognised since Krugman in 2008. I also share the credit concern about Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum. That omission weakens a prize framed around the empirical facts, and the committee would have to frame the citation around the theory of selection and gains from trade in order to keep it coherent. My other reservation is that welfare conclusions depend on functional-form assumptions such as Pareto productivity. I think that makes B021 a strong alternative, and I would support it if B001 stalls on attribution, but I weigh B001's cleaner three-person functional separation and its direct policy use more heavily.

uncertainties: Whether the committee can settle on Taylor, Woodford and Calvo or will insist on including Gali, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum or Smets, which would shift both attribution and citation.
How much weight to give the framework's mixed fit in the post-2021 inflation episode, and the evidence for state-dependent pricing, against its role as a benchmark for policy analysis.
Whether Bresnahan's claim in B015 should displace one of the BLP authors, and whether B015 should be judged as a toolkit contribution or a discovery.
Whether the framing of B021 can credit the empirical firm-level pioneers (Bernard, Jensen, Eaton, Kortum) who are not on this ballot.
statement.conflict_note: Profile-based connections to disclose, not adjudicated: I co-authored with committee chair John Hassler and former chair Tore Ellingsen on 'Menu Costs and Asymmetric Price Adjustment' (IJIO 2026), which is adjacent to the price-setting topics in B001. My research field is industrial organization and international trade, so I have field proximity to B015 and B021. None of the candidates credited on the shortlist appears among my listed co-authors. The profile notes a public family relationship with a Swedish political leader, but nothing in it bears on these scientific candidates and I give it no weight.
